messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi is a 36-year-old accountant who grew up in a South Asian household in New Jersey, the eldest son of parents whose marriage he now describes as a war zone. He remembers the sounds best—the crash of a dinner plate against the kitchen wall, his mother’s sharp intake of breath before she started screaming, the thud of his father’s fist against the wooden dining table. He was six years old the first time he witnessed his father shove his mother so hard she hit the refrigerator and slid to the floor. He stood in the doorway of his bedroom, frozen, unable to cry out or run. He never told anyone. No one ever came. And no one ever held his father accountable. That absence of consequence has become a fixed truth for Ravi: the people who cause harm simply walk away, and the world does nothing to stop them.

Now, thirty years later, Ravi’s body still lives in that doorway. His shoulders are permanently hunched, his jaw clenched, his hands cold and damp even in warm weather. He describes his body as being on constant alert, as though a switch inside him is stuck in the on position. When a coworker drops a stack of files in the office, Ravi’s heart slams against his ribs so hard he has to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he stands gripping the sink, trying to breathe. He has learned to scan every room he enters—the break room, the grocery store, his own apartment—for the angles where someone could be cornered, for the tone of voice that precedes a raised hand. He cannot relax. He cannot remember what it felt like to be happy. He used to be the kind of person who laughed easily, who hosted Diwali dinners for friends, who looked forward to weekends. Now he describes himself as someone who is always miserable, hollowed out, waiting for the next bad thing to happen because he has learned that he cannot stop it.

The memory of his childhood home does not come to him in words. When he tries to talk about it in therapy, his throat closes. He can see the floral pattern on the living room curtains, smell the curry his mother was cooking, feel the vibration of the slammed door through his small feet—but he cannot string the story together. The terror returns whole and wordless, a full-body flash that drops him back into that hallway without warning. A raised voice in a restaurant, the sound of a chair scraping against a floor, the particular way a man’s hand tightens around a glass: any of these can trigger the memory instantly, and he is six years old again, helpless, watching.

His avoidance has become a structure he lives inside. He stopped dating after his divorce three years ago, certain that any intimacy would eventually lead to the same kind of rage he grew up watching. He keeps his conversations at work shallow, deflecting when colleagues ask about his weekend. He has stopped attending family gatherings because his uncle’s booming voice, even when joking, sends him into a state of hypervigilance that lasts for hours. The consequence is a narrowing life: he goes to the office, he returns to his apartment, he watches television with the volume low so he can hear any unexpected noise. He has not visited his parents in two years.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a moment at his desk last month. A senior partner walked past and slapped a hand on his cubicle wall in greeting. Ravi shot out of his chair, papers flying, heart pounding, and stood there shaking while the partner stared at him. He could not explain himself. He could not say what he was afraid of. Later that night, alone in his apartment, he realized he did not want to spend the rest of his life that way—startled, silent, waiting. He is terrified that therapy will force him to put the memory into words, something he has never been able to do. But he is more terrified of staying the way he is, trapped in a body that still believes it is six years old and standing in a doorway, with no one coming to help.
